messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Public Transport: Bus riding, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Malai was twenty-seven years old, a journalist for a regional news outlet in the Pacific Northwest, and he had spent the last eighteen months trying to disappear inside his own life. The relationship that had nearly killed him had ended two years ago, but the man who had done it—a fellow journalist, older, charismatic, someone Malai had trusted completely—still existed in the same professional world. That was the problem. The newsroom was a small ecosystem, and Malai had learned that safety was not something other people could guarantee for you.

The physical abuse had escalated slowly, the way these things often do. What began as sharp words during arguments became a hand gripping his arm too tightly, then a shove against a wall, then a punch to the ribs while Malai was pinned on the bed. He remembered the precise moment he had understood he was in real danger: he had been trying to leave the apartment, and his partner had blocked the door, then slammed him back against the kitchen counter. Malai’s lower back had struck the edge of the granite, and a searing pain had shot through his kidneys. He had crumpled, and his partner had stood over him, breathing hard, and said, “See what you make me do.” In that moment, Malai had believed it. He had believed he was inadequate, that he had provoked this, that if he were a better partner—more attentive, less argumentative, less himself—none of this would have happened.

That belief had not faded. It had calcified. In the months after he finally left, Malai had found himself endlessly replaying the relationship, sifting through every interaction for the thing he had done wrong. He would lie awake at three in the morning, his body rigid, running through the same loop: the text he should not have sent, the tone he should not have used, the boundary he should not have set. He never allowed himself to feel anger toward his ex-partner. That emotion felt dangerous, like a door that should stay locked. Instead, he turned the anger inward, and when that became unbearable, he stopped eating. Food felt like a need he did not deserve to meet. He would go entire days on coffee and a single granola bar, telling himself he was just not hungry, though his hands trembled and his concentration frayed.

His body had become a map of the event. When a memory returned—and it returned often, without warning, with a vividness that made the present moment dissolve—he would feel the exact pain in his lower back, the bruising pressure of a hand on his chest, the sensation of being pinned. The memory did not feel like something that had happened. It felt like something that was happening, right now, in the room with him. When it came, he had to stop whatever he was doing—mid-sentence, mid-edit, mid-walk—and wait for it to pass, his heart pounding, his breath shallow, his whole body braced for a blow that had already landed.

Public transport had become impossible. The bus was a confined space full of strangers, and Malai could not sit with his back to anyone. He would stand near the exit, his eyes scanning the passengers, cataloguing every man who boarded, his body tensing. He was certain that any one of them could be a threat. He had learned that people you trusted could hurt you; strangers were just people you had not yet given the chance. Being alone with any man—a colleague in an elevator, a neighbour in the hallway, a source for an interview—sent his heart into a sprint. He had started requesting that his interviews be conducted by phone or video call, and his editor had noticed. Malai had said he was trying to be more efficient, but the lie felt thin even to him.

At night, he woke repeatedly, his eyes snapping open in the dark, listening. He would check the locks on his apartment door, then check them again, then stand in the hallway and listen for footsteps that were not there. His girlfriend, who had been patient and bewildered, would ask what he was afraid of. He could not explain it in a way that made sense. Even when she held him and said, “You are safe,” he did not believe it. He could not believe it. Safety was not a fact he could absorb; it was a feeling that had been permanently removed from his body.

What had brought him to seek help, finally, was not the fear or the pain or the hunger. It was the story he had been assigned to write—a profile of a local politician—and the politician had asked to meet for coffee. Alone. In a café. Malai had sat in his car outside the café for twenty minutes, his hands gripping the steering wheel, and then he had driven home and called in sick. He had spent the rest of the day in his apartment, not eating, not moving, replaying the moment he had failed to walk through a door. He was afraid that he was becoming someone who could no longer do his job. He was afraid that the man who had hurt him had taken more than he had realised. And he was afraid that if he let himself feel the anger he had never allowed himself to feel, it would consume everything.
